Validating the method on 24 AuriDESI mock catalogs (six Auriga halos at four viewing angles), we find that it overestimates the enclosed mass by $\sim\!15\%$ at 80\,kpc, and correct our results accordingly. We obtain $M(<80\,{\rm kpc}) = 0.64^{+0.06}_{-0.06}$ and $0.53^{+0.05}_{-0.05} \times 10^{12}\,M_\odot$ for BHBs and RRLs, respectively, while including Sagittarius stream stars lowers these masses by $\sim\!10$\%. Extrapolating to 100\,kpc, we obtain $M(<100\,{\rm kpc}) = 0.74^{+0.07}_{-0.07}$ and $0.62^{+0.06}_{-0.07} \times 10^{12}\,M_\odot$, and anchoring an NFW halo to our GME constraints at 65\,kpc yields virial masses of $M_{200} = 1.12^{+0.14}_{-0.12}$ and $0.89^{+0.11}_{-0.10} \times 10^{12}\,M_\odot$. BHBs yield systematically higher masses than RRLs across the full radial range, reflecting the impact of tracer choice even within a single method. This work is part of a wider DESI DR2 Key Project effort to measure the Milky Way mass and constrain systematics arising from different samples and methodologies.

AI.tldr: Using DESI DR2 BHB and RR Lyrae halo tracers at 50–80 kpc and a hierarchical Bayesian mass estimator validated on mock catalogs, the authors measure the Milky Way enclosed and virial mass, finding BHBs systematically yield ~20% higher masses than RRLs.
AI.motivation: Precise Milky Way mass measurements are essential as a benchmark for galaxy formation models and ΛCDM, yet results vary with tracer sample and methodology. The work exploits the larger DESI DR2 catalogs and quantifies systematic biases (tracer choice, stream contamination, method bias).
AI.method: 279 blue horizontal-branch and 213 RR Lyrae stars at 50–80 kpc from Galactic center, roughly twice the DR1 sample size. Applied the Galactic Mass Estimator (GME), a hierarchical Bayesian framework with power-law potential and tracer density, incorporating distance/velocity uncertainties. Validated on 24 AuriDESI mock catalogs (6 Auriga halos × 4 viewing angles), correcting a ~15% mass overestimate at 80 kpc. Extrapolation to 100 kpc and NFW halo fitting anchored at 65 kpc.
AI.result: M(<80 kpc) = 0.64 ± 0.06 (BHB) and 0.53 ± 0.05 (RRL) ×10^12 M_sun; including Sagittarius stream stars lowers masses ~10%. M(<100 kpc) = 0.74 ± 0.07 and 0.62 ± 0.06/0.07 ×10^12 M_sun; NFW virial masses M200 = 1.12 ± 0.14/0.12 and 0.89 ± 0.11/0.10 ×10^12 M_sun.
AI.conclusion: BHBs systematically yield higher masses than RRLs across the full radial range, demonstrating significant tracer-dependent systematics even within a single method. The study forms part of the DESI DR2 Key Project to measure the Milky Way mass and constrain systematics from different samples and methodologies.

title: The formation and evolution of Wolf-Rayet stars with temperature-dependent winds
comment: 11 pages, 9 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society (MNRAS)
summary: Massive stars strongly influence their environments through their radiation, stellar winds and core-collapse supernovae, while their own evolution is strongly shaped by wind mass loss. Wolf-Rayet (WR) stars are characterised by strong, optically thick winds, and the implementation of these winds remains an important uncertainty in stellar evolution models. Recent hydrodynamically consistent atmosphere calculations predict WR mass-loss rates that depend strongly on the temperature at the wind-launching region. We investigate the effects of incorporating these latest theoretical WR wind prescriptions into single and binary stellar evolution models at Milky Way, Large Magellanic Cloud and Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC) metallicities. We find that the temperature dependence of the WR wind can significantly alter the evolution of stars near the threshold for WR formation. In particular, an implementation that transitions from a hydrogen rich WNL wind prescription to a classical WR wind driven by the hot iron opacity bump causes some SMC-metallicity models to spend an extended period at temperatures of approximately 70 to 90 kK. This produces a concentration of models in the temperature range occupied by most observed SMC WR stars, a feature that has previously been difficult to explain with stellar evolution models. Our results demonstrate that incorporating physically motivated, temperature dependent WR winds can improve the agreement between stellar evolution models and observed WR populations.

AI.tldr: Incorporating temperature-dependent, hydrodynamically consistent Wolf-Rayet (WR) wind prescriptions into single and binary stellar evolution models at Milky Way, LMC and SMC metallicities shows that the WR wind temperature dependence can substantially reshape evolution near the WR-formation threshold, producing a concentration of SMC models at 70–90 kK that matches observed SMC WR stars.
AI.motivation: WR stars have strong, optically thick winds whose treatment is a major uncertainty in stellar evolution models. Recent hydrodynamically consistent atmosphere calculations predict WR mass-loss rates that depend strongly on the temperature at the wind-launching region, and the impact of adopting these prescriptions on stellar evolution has not been assessed.
AI.method: The authors implement the latest theoretical WR wind prescriptions in single and binary stellar evolution models at solar (Milky Way), LMC and SMC metallicities, and examine how the temperature dependence of the WR mass-loss rate affects the evolutionary tracks of stars near the threshold for WR formation.
AI.result: The WR wind temperature dependence significantly alters evolution near the WR-formation threshold. In particular, a prescription transitioning from a hydrogen-rich WNL wind to a classical WR wind driven by the hot iron opacity bump causes some SMC-metallicity models to spend an extended period at roughly 70–90 kK, concentrating models in the temperature range occupied by most observed SMC WR stars—a feature previously difficult to reproduce.
AI.conclusion: Physically motivated, temperature-dependent WR wind prescriptions improve agreement between stellar evolution models and observed WR populations, resolving a long-standing discrepancy in the SMC WR temperature distribution.

title: Identifying Compact Object Candidates using Gaia DR3 Astrometric Accelerations and Jerks
comment: 16 pages, 7 figures, submitted to AAS journals, comments welcome
summary: Gaia Data Release 3 (DR3) provides astrometric measurements for more than a billion sources, hundreds of thousands of which have non-single-star astrometric solutions that indicate deviations from linear proper motion. Although sources with orbital solutions have been extensively inspected for compact objects via the astrometric mass function, two other solution types--the 7-parameter constant-acceleration solutions characterized by $\dot{\mathbfμ}$, and the 9-parameter variable-acceleration solutions characterized by $\dot{\mathbfμ}$ and $\ddot{\mathbfμ}$--have not been as carefully explored. In this work, we develop a methodology for selecting sources within the Gaia DR3 9-parameter non-single-star astrometric solutions that are most likely to host massive compact companions. We assume that a source is the luminous star in a binary orbit around a dark object and derive analytic expressions for the sky-projected accelerations and jerks for three binary populations with different orbit approximations: inclined eccentric, face-on eccentric, and face-on circular. Using POSYDON, we develop a fourth, more realistic population of binaries, each consisting of a luminous star and a black hole. For each population, we address observational biases using gaiamock and select only the systems it fits with a 9-parameter solution. We find that binaries likely to host massive compact companions can be identified from the characteristic joint astrometric accelerations and jerks exhibited by the luminous stars, despite 9-parameter fits under-constraining full orbits. Finally, to illustrate the utility of our approach, we analyze a historical object of interest, HD 12871, and examine 9-parameter fits of Gaia BH3-like binaries.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a methodology for identifying Gaia DR3 9-parameter (variable-acceleration) non-single-star astrometric solutions most likely to host massive dark companions, using analytic acceleration/jerk signatures validated with synthetic binary populations and gaiamock observational bias modeling.
AI.motivation: Gaia DR3 contains hundreds of thousands of non-single-star astrometric solutions. Orbital (7-parameter-type) solutions have been extensively mined for compact objects via the astrometric mass function, but constant-acceleration (7-parameter, characterized by proper-motion dot $\dot{\mathbf{\mu}}$) and variable-acceleration (9-parameter, characterized by $\dot{\mathbf{\mu}}$ and $\ddot{\mathbf{\mu}}$) solutions have been comparatively neglected. Since these solution types can be produced by luminous stars orbiting unseen massive compact companions, a systematic selection framework is needed to find compact-object candidates among them.
AI.method: The authors assume a luminous star orbits a dark object and derive analytic expressions for sky-projected accelerations and jerks for three idealized binary populations with different orbital approximations: inclined eccentric, face-on eccentric, and face-on circular. A fourth, more realistic population of luminous-star/black-hole binaries is generated with the POSYDON population-synthesis code. Observational biases are then addressed by injecting each population into gaiamock and retaining only systems that are fit with a 9-parameter solution. The resulting joint acceleration-jerk signature in the luminous star is used as a selection diagnostic.
AI.result: Binaries likely to host massive compact companions can be identified from the characteristic joint astrometric acceleration and jerk signatures imprinted on the luminous star, even though 9-parameter fits substantially under-constrain the full orbit. The approach is demonstrated on the historical object of interest HD 12871 and on 9-parameter fits of Gaia BH3-like binaries.
AI.conclusion: Joint acceleration-jerk diagnostics provide a viable selection channel for massive compact companions among Gaia DR3 9-parameter non-single-star solutions, complementing the astrometric mass function used for orbital solutions, and the framework can be applied to both archival candidates and BH3-like systems.

title: Revisiting the Stellar-Dynamical Mass of the Central Black Hole in NGC 3227
comment: Submitted to ApJ
summary: We present a new stellar-dynamical mass for the supermassive black hole in the nearby Seyfert galaxy NGC 3227. We determined the line-of-sight velocity distributions of stars in the nuclear region of NGC 3227 using archival spatially-resolved $K$-band spectra obtained with NIFS at Gemini Observatory. The surface brightness profile of the galaxy is described by four components, measured from a WFC3 F547M image from the Hubble Space Telescope. We constructed dynamical models using the Schwarzschild orbit-superposition method implemented in the open-source code $\texttt{FORSTAND}$. We find a best-fit black hole mass of $M_{\mathrm{BH}}$=$(1.2\pm0.5) \times 10^7$ $M_{\odot}$. This mass is consistent with a previous mass from R. I. Davies et al. based on stellar dynamics using orbit-based modeling, but our results make use of higher signal-to-noise data from which the higher-order moments of the stellar LOSVDs are constrained, thus providing a more precise $M_{\mathrm{BH}}$. Our result is also consistent with the $M_{\mathrm{BH}}$ constraint from velocity-resolved reverberation mapping reported by M. C. Bentz et al.. And while our best-fit mass is slightly smaller than the mass constraint from gas-dynamical modeling reported by E. K. S. Hicks & M. A. Malkan (after scaling to the same adopted distance), they are within 2$σ$ of each other. Direct comparisons of black hole masses from different techniques are rare but crucial to ensure all black hole masses are on the same scale, and to identify and minimize the uncertainties and possible sources of bias associated with each technique.

AI.tldr: A stellar-dynamical measurement of the supermassive black hole mass in NGC 3227 yields M_BH = (1.2 ± 0.5) × 10^7 M_sun, consistent with prior stellar-dynamical and reverberation-mapping estimates and within 2σ of gas-dynamical results.
AI.motivation: There is a need for direct comparisons of black hole masses derived from different techniques to ensure all masses are on a common scale and to identify and minimize uncertainties and potential biases associated with each method. NGC 3227 is a well-studied nearby Seyfert galaxy that allows such cross-technique comparison.
AI.method: Line-of-sight velocity distributions (LOSVDs) of stars in the nuclear region were extracted from archival spatially-resolved K-band spectra taken with NIFS at Gemini. The surface brightness profile was modeled with four components measured from a WFC3 F547M HST image. Schwarzschild orbit-superposition dynamical models were built using the open-source code FORSTAND.
AI.result: The best-fit black hole mass is M_BH = (1.2 ± 0.5) × 10^7 M_sun. This agrees with the earlier stellar-dynamical orbit-based mass of Davies et al., while providing a more precise value owing to higher signal-to-noise data that constrain the higher-order moments of the stellar LOSVDs. It is also consistent with the velocity-resolved reverberation-mapping constraint of Bentz et al., and lies slightly below but within 2σ of the gas-dynamical mass of Hicks & Malkan after scaling to the same adopted distance.
AI.conclusion: The new stellar-dynamical mass for NGC 3227 is precise and consistent with independent stellar-dynamical, reverberation-mapping, and (within 2σ) gas-dynamical estimates, supporting cross-calibration of black hole mass measurement techniques and underscoring the value of such direct comparisons for identifying and minimizing method-specific systematics.

title: The impact of Population III stars on the elemental enrichment of ultra-faint galaxies in the FIRE-3 zoom-in simulations
comment: 22 pages, 13 figures. Submitted to ApJ
summary: The observed stellar mass-metallicity relation for ultra-faint galaxies in the Local Group (LG) is in tension with many theoretical predictions, suggesting the need for modified or additional channels of elemental enrichment at low metallicities. We present a suite of FIRE-3 cosmological baryonic zoom-in simulations of isolated ultra-faint galaxies run to z=0 (maximum baryonic resolution ~ 30 Msun, 0.1 pc) and LMC-mass environments (maximum baryonic resolution ~ 110 Msun, 0.5 pc), with different sub-grid models for Population III stars. Under our Pop. III model(s), star particles forming below a critical metallicity Z_crit represent an initial mass function (IMF) consisting of only massive stars (8-100 Msun). We examine how various stellar feedback processes impact the star formation histories (SFHs) and elemental abundances of ultra-faint galaxies. We find that our Pop. III model variants introduce an effective metallicity floor in ultra-faints at z=0, at Z_floor ~ 1e-5 Zsun to 1e-3 Zsun or [Fe/H]_floor ~ -7 to -5 depending on the model. However, simply including the Pop. III model does not systematically guarantee that all (or even most) ultra-faints enrich up to [Fe/H] ~ -2.5 to fully resolve the tension with the observed mass-metallicity relation, even though we obtain some galaxies at that level. Crucially, the ultra-faints that do enrich in [Fe/H] to this level observed in the LG have extended SFHs after Pop. III enrichment and significant iron enrichment from white dwarf (Type Ia) supernovae, indicating that iron enrichment from Pop. III alone is not sufficient. We also examine the ways in which early-time Pop. III feedback impacts the metallicity distributions and [Mg/Fe] abundance ratios in ultra-faint galaxies, and make a prediction for the stellar mass - [Mg/H] metallicity relation from our simulations.

AI.tldr: FIRE-3 zoom-in simulations with Population III sub-grid models show that Pop. III stars set a metallicity floor in ultra-faint galaxies, but resolving the observed mass-metallicity tension requires extended star formation and late Type Ia iron enrichment.
AI.motivation: The observed stellar mass-metallicity relation of Local Group ultra-faint galaxies conflicts with theoretical predictions, implying missing or modified low-metallicity enrichment channels. The authors test whether Population III stars can account for this.
AI.method: A suite of FIRE-3 cosmological baryonic zoom-in simulations of isolated ultra-faint galaxies to z=0 (~30 Msun, 0.1 pc max baryonic resolution) and LMC-mass environments (~110 Msun, 0.5 pc), varying sub-grid Pop. III models in which star particles forming below Z_crit adopt a massive-only IMF (8-100 Msun). Stellar feedback effects on SFHs and abundances are analyzed.
AI.result: Pop. III variants impose an effective metallicity floor at Z ~ 1e-5 to 1e-3 Zsun ([Fe/H] ~ -7 to -5). However, including Pop. III does not systematically enrich most ultra-faints to [Fe/H] ~ -2.5. Galaxies reaching this level exhibit extended SFHs after Pop. III enrichment and substantial Type Ia iron contribution. Early Pop. III feedback shapes metallicity distributions and [Mg/Fe] ratios; a prediction for the stellar mass-[Mg/H] relation is provided.
AI.conclusion: Pop. III enrichment alone is insufficient to resolve the mass-metallicity tension; extended star formation histories and white dwarf Type Ia iron enrichment are essential for ultra-faints to reach observed metallicities.

title: Mock CSST NUV-NIR imaging of TNG50 galaxies with resolved stellar populations
comment: 14 pages, 13 figures, 5 tables, accepted for publication in A&A
summary: Aims. We aim to develop a framework for producing CSST-like mock images of resolved stellar populations from simulated galaxies, demonstrated here using two TNG50 galaxies as illustrative test cases. Methods. Starting from simulated galaxies from TNG50, we use the population synthesis code TRILEGAL to sample individual stars from star particles, retaining bright stars explicitly and treating the remaining unresolved light, including faint stellar light and nebular emission from star-forming regions, as a diffuse background component of the galaxy. Based on the dust distribution inferred from the gas mass and metallicity of gas cells, we use the radiative transfer (RT) code SKIRT to construct the dust model. From this model, we compute the line-of-sight extinction for individual stars, while image-level transmission maps for the diffuse light are derived through RT simulations. For young stars still embedded in their natal molecular clouds, we additionally include birth-cloud attenuation. The resulting dust-attenuated stellar catalogues and diffuse-light images are then processed with the CSST simulation pipeline, which applies PSF convolution, sky background, and instrumental noise. Results. Our framework produces mock CSST images for both a spiral galaxy and a dwarf irregular galaxy from TNG50 in the seven photometric bands. The mock images combine resolved stars, unresolved diffuse light, and dust attenuation within a unified framework, and include the main observational effects expected for the survey. The images are provided with known astrometric and photometric calibration information, and are intended as realistic image-level inputs for subsequent source detection, photometric recovery, and completeness analyses of resolved stellar populations. The framework is designed to be adaptable to other hydrodynamic simulations and observing configurations.

AI.tldr: The authors build a pipeline that turns TNG50 simulated galaxies into realistic CSST-like mock images. Individual bright stars are sampled via TRILEGAL, faint unresolved light is treated as a diffuse background, dust is modeled with SKIRT, and everything is passed through the CSST simulation pipeline to produce seven-band images with known calibration.
AI.motivation: There is a need for image-level mock data that realistically represent resolved stellar populations as CSST will observe them, so that source detection, photometric recovery, and completeness studies can be validated against simulations grounded in physically motivated galaxy models.
AI.method: Starting from TNG50 galaxies, the population synthesis code TRILEGAL samples individual stars from star particles, keeping bright stars explicit and folding remaining faint stellar and nebular emission into a diffuse background. A dust model is built with the radiative transfer code SKIRT using dust masses inferred from gas mass and metallicity of gas cells. Line-of-sight extinction is computed for individual stars, image-level transmission maps for diffuse light come from RT simulations, and birth-cloud attenuation is added for young embedded stars. The attenuated catalogues and diffuse images are then run through the CSST simulation pipeline (PSF convolution, sky background, instrumental noise).
AI.result: The framework yields mock CSST images in seven photometric bands for a TNG50 spiral galaxy and a dwarf irregular galaxy, combining resolved stars, unresolved diffuse light, and dust attenuation in one unified framework. Images incorporate the main expected observational effects and ship with known astrometric and photometric calibration information.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides realistic image-level inputs for source detection, photometric recovery, and completeness analyses of resolved stellar populations, and is designed to be adaptable to other hydrodynamic simulations and observing configurations.

title: Spectroscopy-informed Deep Learning Searches for Photometric Little Red Dots in JWST Surveys
comment: 11 figures (9 in the main text and 2 additional in appendix), 5 tables, to appear in ApJS soon 35 new LRD candidates with NIRSpec/PRISM are identified
summary: Little Red Dots (LRDs) are a population of compact, red sources discovered at high redshift with JWST that exhibit distinctive V-shaped spectral energy distributions (SEDs). Existing LRD samples are typically identified using a variety of color-based selection criteria, which can lead to differences in the populations recovered by different studies. We develop a cross-modal machine-learning framework that combines matched NIRCam imaging and NIRSpec/PRISM spectroscopy to transfer spectroscopic information into imaging-based representations, enabling LRD identification from JWST/NIRCam imaging alone. Applied to spectroscopically observed high-redshift galaxies previously classified as non-LRDs, our model identifies 35 new LRD candidates. The majority satisfy at least one independent LRD color selection criterion, and among the 13 candidates with medium- or high-resolution NIRSpec grating spectra, 10 exhibit broad H$α$ emission - a hallmark of LRDs. We further apply the classifier to public NIRCam imaging from the Dawn JWST Archive and two independent JWST surveys, yielding 357 and 23 additional LRD candidates, respectively. The candidates recovered by our method span a broader range of observed SED properties than those in existing samples, suggesting that current color-selected samples may not fully capture the diversity of LRD-like systems present in JWST surveys. Our findings highlight the value of spectroscopy-informed photometric classification as a powerful strategy for systematically mining large-area JWST imaging datasets and provide a practical framework for future studies of this emerging population.

AI.tldr: A cross-modal ML framework transfers NIRSpec spectroscopy into NIRCam imaging representations to identify Little Red Dots from imaging alone, recovering new candidates that color-based selections miss.
AI.motivation: Little Red Dots (LRDs) are compact, high-redshift sources with distinctive V-shaped SEDs found by JWST, but existing samples rely on heterogeneous color-based selection criteria, so different studies recover inconsistent populations and likely miss diverse LRD-like systems.
AI.method: The authors build a cross-modal machine-learning framework that combines matched NIRCam imaging and NIRSpec/PRISM spectroscopy, transferring spectroscopic information into imaging-based representations so that LRD identification is possible from NIRCam imaging alone. The classifier is then applied to spectroscopically observed non-LRD galaxies and to public NIRCam imaging from the Dawn JWST Archive and two independent JWST surveys.
AI.result: The model identifies 35 new LRD candidates among previously non-LRD classified galaxies; most satisfy at least one independent LRD color criterion, and 10 of the 13 with medium/high-resolution NIRSpec grating spectra show broad H-alpha emission, an LRD hallmark. Application to public imaging yields 357 and 23 additional candidates from Dawn and two independent surveys, respectively, spanning broader SED properties than existing samples.
AI.conclusion: Spectroscopy-informed photometric classification is a powerful strategy for systematically mining large-area JWST imaging, and current color-selected LRD samples may not fully capture the diversity of LRD-like systems, motivating broader survey-scale searches.

title: Aperture-dependent [O III] profile variability: Clues to the nature of double-peaked narrow emission lines
comment: 8 pages,3 figures, accepted by A&A
summary: We propose a simple and practical aperture-dependent method for investigating the physical origin of double-peaked narrow emission lines (DPNELs). Spectroscopic observations obtained from different apertures probe different spatial regions and therefore different gas kinematics within the narrow line region (NLR). Consequently, changes in the profiles of DPNELs observed with different apertures can provide important constraints on their physical origins. We applied this method to SDSS J0941 by comparing spectra obtained from the SDSS, DESI, and LAMOST surveys. Significant differences are found in the double-peaked profiles of the different spectra, demonstrating that aperture effects can strongly influence the integrated DPNEL profiles. The AGN model, where the two nuclei lie in a plane perpendicular to the line of sight, can qualitatively explain the asymmetric sampling of the two NLRs, but it cannot explain the different peak separations of different spectra. The observed asymmetric evolution of the two components disfavors a simple AGN-driven outflow and a rotating disk-like NLR scenario. Of the models considered, only a more complex non-axisymmetric rotating NLR provides a self-consistent explanation for the observed aperture-dependent variations. In this scenario, the blueshifted emitting region is more compact and remains largely enclosed by the smaller aperture, resulting in an increased line width with little change in flux. In contrast, the redshifted emitting region is more spatially extended and is therefore more strongly affected by the reduced aperture, leading to pronounced decreases in both flux and line width. Our results illustrate the diagnostic potential of combining multi-aperture spectroscopic surveys to study DPNEL origins, while highlighting the difficulty of distinguishing between physical scenarios.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce an aperture-dependent spectroscopic method to diagnose the physical origin of double-peaked narrow emission lines, and apply it to SDSS J0941 by comparing SDSS, DESI, and LAMOST spectra, finding that only a complex non-axisymmetric rotating NLR model self-consistently explains the aperture-dependent profile variations.
AI.motivation: Double-peaked narrow emission lines can arise from several distinct physical scenarios (dual AGN, outflows, rotating disks), and single-aperture spectra cannot easily discriminate among them. Because different apertures probe different spatial regions and gas kinematics in the NLR, comparing spectra from differing apertures offers a new observational constraint on the origin of DPNELs.
AI.method: A simple, practical aperture-dependent method: compare DPNEL profiles of the same object (SDSS J0941) obtained from surveys with different aperture sizes—SDSS, DESI, and LAMOST—and test each candidate physical model against the observed aperture-dependent changes in the two line components.
AI.result: Significant differences are found among the double-peaked profiles from the different spectra, showing aperture effects can strongly influence integrated DPNEL profiles. The dual-AGN model (two nuclei in a plane perpendicular to the line of sight) can qualitatively explain asymmetric sampling of the two NLRs but not the differing peak separations. The asymmetric evolution of the two components disfavors a simple AGN-driven outflow and a rotating disk-like NLR. Only a non-axisymmetric rotating NLR model explains the data self-consistently: the blueshifted region is compact and largely enclosed by the smaller aperture (increased line width, little flux change), while the redshifted region is spatially extended and strongly affected by the reduced aperture (decreases in both flux and line width).
AI.conclusion: Aperture-dependent spectroscopy across multi-aperture surveys has diagnostic power for DPNEL origins, but distinguishing between physical scenarios remains difficult, as several models can partially reproduce the observations.

title: Evolutionary Map of the Universe (EMU): Selection of active galactic nuclei and star-formation emission with machine-learning techniques
comment: Accepted for publication in A&A, 19 pages, 20 figures, and two tables
summary: Sources detected by recent large-area radio surveys require robust classification and characterisation. The Evolutionary Map of the Universe (EMU) is a prime example of machine-learning (ML) techniques efficiently enriching existing catalogues with classifications and derived physical properties that would be impractical to obtain from spectroscopy or colour selection alone. We aim to build a labelled sample of sources in the EMU pilot survey (EMU-PS, at 944 MHz, with rms ~ 30 uJy/beam over 270 deg2 in the southern sky) classified as being dominated by active galactic nuclei (AGNs) or non-AGN processes including star-formation. We will then use this sample to examine radio properties and redshift-dependent trends. We applied a pre-trained multi-stage ML pipeline to optical-to-infrared photometry of EMU-PS sources to derive classifications and photometric redshifts, which we used to compute additional radio properties, including luminosities. We increase the known number of AGNs and non-AGNs in the EMU-PS by more than a factor of 15 (recall 96 %) up to z ~ 5, and by nearly a factor of 100 (recall 94 %) for z > 1, respectively. In extrapolating these numbers for the full EMU survey, we expect to recover more than 3.4 million AGN candidates. A non-negligible low-redshift subsample of selected non-AGNs shows radio luminosities in excess of those expected from star formation alone, revealing detachment between photometric and radio classification. Radio-derived properties show expected trends for luminosities and a lack of evolution for in-band (800-1088 MHz) spectral indices. The ML-based pipeline provides a scalable way to produce large catalogues for the ongoing EMU survey and future Square Kilometre Array observations and reveals that multi-wavelength analysis can uncover radio populations and trends often missed by colour cuts or spectroscopy alone.

AI.tldr: A pre-trained multi-stage ML pipeline classifies EMU pilot survey radio sources into AGN and non-AGN and derives photometric redshifts, expanding labelled samples by 15–100×. Extrapolation predicts >3.4 million AGN candidates for the full EMU survey, and a low-redshift non-AGN subsample shows excess radio luminosity, revealing detachment between photometric and radio classification.
AI.motivation: Large-area radio surveys such as EMU produce vast source catalogues that cannot feasibly be classified or characterised via spectroscopy or colour selection alone. A robust, scalable method is needed to label sources as AGN- or star-formation-dominated and to derive physical properties for population and redshift-dependent studies.
AI.method: Applied a pre-trained multi-stage ML pipeline to optical-to-infrared photometry of EMU-PS sources (944 MHz, rms ~30 µJy/beam, 270 deg², southern sky) to obtain AGN/non-AGN classifications and photometric redshifts, from which additional radio properties including luminosities were computed.
AI.result: Known AGN and non-AGN samples in EMU-PS were increased by >15× (recall 96%) up to z ~5 and by ~100× (recall 94%) at z >1, respectively; extrapolation implies >3.4 million AGN candidates from full EMU. A non-negligible low-redshift non-AGN subsample exhibits radio luminosities exceeding star-formation expectations. Luminosities follow expected trends and in-band (800–1088 MHz) spectral indices show no evolution.
AI.conclusion: The ML pipeline offers a scalable route to large catalogues for the ongoing EMU survey and future SKA observations, and demonstrates that multi-wavelength analysis can recover radio populations and trends missed by colour cuts or spectroscopy alone.

title: A brief overview of the baryon cycle in galaxies
summary: Galaxy formation and evolution is governed by the continuous exchange of gas between the cosmic web, the circumgalactic medium (CGM), and the interstellar medium (ISM) of galaxies. This brief review summarises our current understanding of this baryon cycle, from the accretion of gas onto galaxies to its conversion into stars, and the feedback processes that regulate the growth of galaxies. Several open questions will be highlighted, that will encourage progresses in cosmological simulations, multiwavelength observations, and theory to resolve.

AI.tldr: A brief review of the galactic baryon cycle—gas accretion from the cosmic web, its conversion into stars via the CGM and ISM, and feedback processes regulating galaxy growth—highlighting open questions for simulations, multiwavelength observations, and theory.
AI.motivation: Galaxy formation and evolution are fundamentally controlled by the continuous exchange of gas among the cosmic web, circumgalactic medium (CGM), and interstellar medium (ISM); a coherent synthesis of this baryon cycle and its remaining uncertainties is needed to guide future progress.
AI.method: Narrative review/synthesis: the abstract describes a brief review that organises current understanding of the baryon cycle along its sequential stages—accretion onto galaxies, conversion into stars, and feedback regulation—and identifies outstanding open questions rather than presenting new data or modelling.
AI.result: The review consolidates the current picture of the baryon cycle and distils the principal open questions; no quantitative findings are reported in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Resolving the highlighted open questions requires combined advances in cosmological simulations, multiwavelength observations, and theory, which will drive progress in understanding galaxy growth.

title: Quiescent galaxies at cosmic noon: from individual element abundances to star formation histories
comment: 8 pages, 2 figures, published on New Astronomy
summary: Understanding the formation and early evolution of massive quiescent galaxies is crucial for a complete picture of galaxy formation in a cosmological context. Such a comprehensive picture can be obtained through measurements of individual elemental abundances, which encode the timescales and physical conditions of their star-formation and assembly histories. While extensive work at low and intermediate redshift has revealed strong correlations between stellar mass, metallicity, and abundance ratios, studies at z ~ 2-3 remain extremely limited. Their faintness and compactness make medium-resolution near-infrared spectroscopy for detailed chemical analysis extremely challenging. We present a science case to measure full elemental abundance patterns in a representative sample of massive quiescent galaxies at cosmic noon, exploiting rest-frame optical absorption features. We show that deriving robust stellar population constraints for these systems requires spectra with S/N ~ 20 per resolution element, together with a spatial resolution comparable to their ~ 0.1 arcsec sizes. We show that such requirements can only be met with a 40m class telescope equipped with a powerful adaptive optics system. In this context, SHARP-NEXUS, in combination with MORFEO-MCAO capabilities, emerges as the only viable ELT instrument capable of enabling this science, providing both the sensitivity and angular resolution needed. Although massive quiescent galaxies are rare at these redshifts, their study can efficiently exploit the instrument's multiplexing by targeting galaxy overdensities and coordinating with surveys of star-forming galaxies. Such synergistic strategies, proven feasible in high-redshift clusters and by multiplex-sharing facilities like 4MOST, would allow SHARP-NEXUS to open a new window on the chemical enrichment of the earliest massive galaxies.

AI.tldr: A science case for measuring full elemental abundance patterns in massive quiescent galaxies at cosmic noon (z ~ 2-3) using rest-frame optical absorption features, requiring S/N ~ 20 per resolution element and ~0.1 arcsec spatial resolution, achievable only with a 40m-class ELT; SHARP-NEXUS combined with MORFEO-MCAO is identified as the sole viable instrument.
AI.motivation: Understanding the formation and early evolution of massive quiescent galaxies is essential for a complete cosmological picture of galaxy formation. Individual elemental abundances encode the timescales and physical conditions of star formation and assembly histories. While low- and intermediate-redshift studies reveal strong mass–metallicity–abundance-ratio correlations, studies at z ~ 2-3 are extremely limited because these galaxies are faint and compact, making medium-resolution near-infrared spectroscopy for detailed chemical analysis highly challenging.
AI.method: Presents a science case for deriving full elemental abundance patterns in a representative sample of massive quiescent galaxies at cosmic noon via rest-frame optical absorption features, and quantifies the observational requirements: spectra with S/N ~ 20 per resolution element and spatial resolution comparable to the ~0.1 arcsec galaxy sizes. Assesses instrument capabilities against these requirements, identifying 40m-class telescopes with powerful adaptive optics as necessary, and evaluates SHARP-NEXUS with MORFEO-MCAO as the enabling ELT instrument. Proposes observing strategies exploiting multiplexing by targeting galaxy overdensities and coordinating with star-forming galaxy surveys.
AI.result: Robust stellar population constraints for these systems require S/N ~ 20 per resolution element and spatial resolution matching the ~0.1 arcsec sizes. These requirements can only be met by a 40m-class telescope with a powerful AO system. SHARP-NEXUS in combination with MORFEO-MCAO is the only viable ELT instrument providing both the needed sensitivity and angular resolution. Although massive quiescent galaxies are rare at these redshifts, multiplexing can be exploited efficiently by targeting overdensities and coordinating with star-forming galaxy surveys, strategies proven feasible in high-redshift clusters and by multiplex-sharing facilities such as 4MOST.
AI.conclusion: SHARP-NEXUS, with MORFEO-MCAO, would open a new window on the chemical enrichment of the earliest massive galaxies, enabling detailed elemental abundance studies of massive quiescent galaxies at cosmic noon that are currently infeasible. Synergistic multiplexing strategies make this rare-population science efficient and feasible.

title: Understanding galaxies and the origin of the golden mass through the study of scaling relations across cosmic history
comment: 13 pages, 2 figures. Accepted for publication in the New Astronomy Special Issue: SHARP Science Book
summary: The total mass distribution in galaxies strongly influences star formation (SF), both directly via gas availability and feedback, and indirectly via the dark matter (DM) potential well. Star formation efficiency peaks at a characteristic stellar mass of $5 \times 10^{10} M_{\odot}$, often termed the "golden mass", where feedback mechanisms minimally affect SF. This scale also appears in other scaling relations: correlations between stellar population gradients, DM fraction, and total mass density slope versus stellar mass all show pronounced minima at the golden mass. How, why, and when does this golden mass emerge during galaxy evolution? Early cosmic epochs ($z > 1.5$) remain largely unexplored, yet they probe the formative stages of galaxy mass assembly. They provide the full redshift baseline needed to constrain the buildup of stellar mass and the efficiency of gas-to-star conversion. By combining high resolution, multiplexing, and a wide field of view, SHARP on the ELT will address these questions, delivering sharper and deeper data than JWST. In this SHARP White Paper contribution, we present a scientific case exploiting these unique characteristics. SHARP will enable precise measurements of stellar population gradients, DM fractions, and total mass density slopes. Using the mIFU mode, SHARP will obtain spatially-resolved stellar population and dynamical maps for galaxies at $z > 1.5$. Reconstructing these observables for early- and late-type systems will allow us to trace the emergence of the golden mass across cosmic time, and to decode the impact of galaxy processes (mergers, SN, and AGN feedback) by comparing observations with cosmological simulations. (abridged)

AI.tldr: This SHARP white paper argues that the ELT's SHARP instrument, using its mIFU mode, can trace the emergence of the "golden mass" ($5\times10^{10}M_\odot$) at $z>1.5$ by measuring stellar population gradients, dark matter fractions, and total mass density slopes for early- and late-type galaxies.
AI.motivation: Star formation efficiency peaks at a characteristic "golden mass" (~5e10 Msun) where feedback minimally affects SF; this scale also shows minima in scaling relations between stellar population gradients, DM fraction, and density slope versus stellar mass. How, why, and when this golden mass emerges is unknown, and early epochs (z>1.5), which probe formative mass assembly, remain largely unexplored.
AI.method: Exploit SHARP on the ELT (high resolution, multiplexing, wide field of view). Using the mIFU mode, obtain spatially resolved stellar population and dynamical maps for galaxies at z>1.5, reconstructing stellar population gradients, DM fractions, and total mass density slopes, and comparing with cosmological simulations to isolate effects of mergers, SN, and AGN feedback.
AI.result: SHARP will deliver sharper and deeper data than JWST, enabling precise spatially-resolved measurements of these observables and tracing the golden mass across cosmic time.
AI.conclusion: SHARP provides the redshift baseline and sensitivity needed to constrain stellar mass buildup and gas-to-star conversion efficiency, decoding the origin and evolution of the golden mass.

title: Supermassive black holes and nuclear star clusters in galaxies: constraining formation and co-evolution with SHARP and MICADO
comment: 8 pages, 1 figure. Contribution to the SHARP Science Book
summary: Nuclear star clusters and supermassive black holes are the dominant compact components in galaxy nuclei. They can coexist within the same system, and their relative prominence traces the history of gas inflow, star formation, and dynamical evolution on parsec scales. Key questions remain open concerning the physical channels that assemble nuclear star clusters, the mass regimes in which supermassive black holes become dynamically dominant, and the conditions under which compact stellar nuclei are suppressed, destroyed, or replaced by cusp-like structures. We describe how near-infrared integral-field spectroscopy with SHARP on the Extremely Large Telescope, combined with high-resolution imaging from MICADO, enables quantitative tests of nuclear formation and evolution scenarios within a unified framework. The joint analysis of stellar dynamics, stellar populations, and nuclear structure allows black-hole masses, internal kinematics of nuclear star clusters, and signatures of gas inflow to be measured consistently within the same systems, and defines the mass and distance ranges where robust constraints can be obtained. Recent discoveries of compact active nuclei at high redshift indicate that efficient black-hole growth can occur in systems with weak or compact stellar components. Although nearby galaxies are not evolutionary analogues of early systems, the diversity of nuclear configurations accessible with SHARP and MICADO provides a local laboratory for isolating the physical mechanisms that regulate the coupled evolution of central black holes and nuclear stellar structures.

AI.tldr: Near-infrared integral-field spectroscopy with SHARP on the ELT, combined with MICADO imaging, enables consistent, quantitative tests of nuclear star cluster formation, black-hole dynamical dominance, and gas-inflow-driven coevolution in a unified framework.
AI.motivation: Nuclear star clusters (NSCs) and supermassive black holes (SMBHs) are the dominant compact nuclear components and can coexist; their relative prominence traces gas inflow, star formation, and dynamical evolution on parsec scales. Open questions concern the physical channels assembling NSCs, the mass regimes where SMBHs become dynamically dominant, and when compact stellar nuclei are suppressed, destroyed, or replaced by cusps.
AI.method: Joint near-infrared integral-field spectroscopy with SHARP on the Extremely Large Telescope plus high-resolution imaging from MICADO, analyzing stellar dynamics, stellar populations, and nuclear structure consistently within the same systems, and mapping the mass and distance ranges yielding robust constraints.
AI.result: The combined SHARP/MICADO analysis allows consistent measurement of black-hole masses, internal kinematics of NSCs, and gas-inflow signatures in the same systems; high-redshift compact active nuclei show efficient black-hole growth can occur in systems with weak or compact stellar components.
AI.conclusion: Although nearby galaxies are not evolutionary analogues of early systems, the diversity of nuclear configurations accessible with SHARP and MICADO constitutes a local laboratory for isolating mechanisms regulating coupled SMBH–nuclear stellar structure evolution.

title: Net Cooling Tables for Cosmological Simulations under Multiple UV/X-ray Background Models
comment: submitted to Astronomy & Computing
summary: We present three sets of net cooling tables for cosmological hydrodynamical simulations, computed with CLOUDY 23.01 for optically thin gas in photoionization equilibrium with three different UV/X-ray background models. Following the element-by-element approach, and in a format compatible with existing tables, we tabulate cooling, heating, and net rates separately for hydrogen and helium over an extended range of helium mass fractions and for 13 heavy elements, together with hydrogen species fractions, electron abundances, and mean particle masses. For gas of Solar composition, the choice of UV/X-ray background has little impact on the net cooling rates at low redshift, but the results increasingly diverge towards high redshift, particularly in diffuse gas near thermal equilibrium. Compared with widely used previous tables, cooling times in this regime differ by up to an order of magnitude at $z \gtrsim 4.6$, and the calculations disagree on whether the gas undergoes net cooling or heating over nearly 10% of the diffuse density-temperature plane at $z \approx 8$, corresponding to the intergalactic medium. These trends persist for gas composed exclusively of hydrogen and helium. The tables provide a consistent framework for assessing the impact of the radiation background on gas cooling in cosmological simulations.

AI.tldr: We release three CLOUDY 23.01 net cooling tables for optically thin, photoionized cosmological gas under three UV/X-ray background models, with per-element rates over extended helium abundances and 13 metals; background choice critically affects high-redshift diffuse gas cooling.
AI.motivation: Cosmological hydrodynamical simulations depend on cooling tables, but widely used tables are based on older CLOUDY versions and a single UV/X-ray background, leaving the radiation-background dependence of net cooling—especially at high redshift—unquantified.
AI.method: Cooling, heating, and net rates are computed with CLOUDY 23.01 for optically thin gas in photoionization equilibrium under three UV/X-ray background models. An element-by-element approach tabulates H and He separately across an extended range of helium mass fractions plus 13 heavy elements, along with H species fractions, electron abundances, and mean particle masses, in a format compatible with existing tables. Solar-composition and pure H/He gas are compared, and results contrasted against previous tables.
AI.result: For Solar-composition gas, the background choice has little effect on net cooling at low redshift but diverges increasingly toward high redshift, particularly in diffuse gas near thermal equilibrium. Cooling times differ from prior tables by up to an order of magnitude at z ≳ 4.6, and the calculations disagree on net cooling versus heating over ~10% of the diffuse density–temperature plane at z ≈ 8 (the intergalactic medium). Trends persist for pure H/He gas.
AI.conclusion: The tables furnish a consistent framework for assessing how the radiation background affects gas cooling in cosmological simulations, showing that background model choice and CLOUDY version materially change high-redshift cooling predictions in diffuse IGM-like gas.

title: AGN Host Galaxies in COSMOS-Web: Linking Structural Evolution and Star Formation Quenching up to $z=5$
comment: 20 pages, 13 figures, submitted to ApJ
summary: The role of active galactic nuclei (AGNs) in the suppression of star formation and structural evolution of galaxies during their transition from star-forming to quiescent systems remains unclear. We analyze 3,955 AGNs selected through five multiwavelength diagnostics at $0<z<5$. Using high-resolution JWST imaging from the COSMOS-Web survey and archival multi-wavelength photometry, we investigate the rest-frame optical size-mass distribution of AGN host galaxies and compare it with those of star-forming galaxies (SFGs) and quiescent galaxies (QGs). We find that the positions of AGN hosts in the size-mass plane depend on both redshift and stellar mass. At $z\gtrsim2$, massive AGN hosts ($M_\star/M_\odot>10^{10.5}$) generally exhibit sizes comparable to those of SFGs despite suppressed star formation. Toward lower redshifts, they increasingly approach the QG size-mass relation, accompanied by declining specific star formation rates (sSFRs) and increasing Sérsic indices. In contrast, lower-mass AGN hosts remain close to the SFG relation across the redshift range. Overall, AGN hosts exhibit relatively mild size evolution, following $R_e\propto(1+z)^{-0.6}$ over $0<z<4$, shallower than that of typical SFGs and QGs. We further examine the relationship between star formation activity and structural compactness in the $Δ\log\mathrm{SFR}_{\mathrm{MS}}$-$ΔΣ_e$ plane. At $z<2.2$, AGN hosts predominantly occupy the compact star-forming and quiescent regions, broadly consistent with the compaction-quenching scenario. At $z>2.2$, however, some AGN hosts exhibit suppressed star formation while retaining relatively extended structures. These findings suggest that some AGN hosts may follow alternative evolutionary pathways in which star formation suppression precedes substantial structural compaction.

AI.tldr: AGN host galaxies at 0<z<5 show size-mass positions that depend on redshift and stellar mass: massive hosts at z>2 are SFG-sized despite suppressed SFR, migrating toward the QG relation at lower z, indicating star formation suppression can precede structural compaction.
AI.motivation: The role of AGNs in quenching star formation and shaping the structural evolution of galaxies transitioning from star-forming to quiescent remains unclear.
AI.method: Analyzes 3,955 AGNs selected via five multiwavelength diagnostics at 0<z<5 using JWST COSMOS-Web high-resolution imaging plus archival photometry; studies the rest-frame optical size-mass distribution of AGN hosts versus SFGs and QGs, the size evolution slope, and the Δlog SFR_MS–ΔΣ_e plane.
AI.result: At z>2, massive AGN hosts (>1e10.5 Msun) have SFG-like sizes despite suppressed star formation; at lower z they approach the QG size-mass relation with declining sSFR and rising Sérsic indices. Low-mass hosts stay near the SFG relation at all z. AGN hosts show mild size evolution, Re ∝ (1+z)^-0.6, shallower than SFGs and QGs. At z<2.2 hosts occupy compact star-forming/quiescent regions (consistent with compaction-quenching); at z>2.2 some show suppressed star formation with extended structures.
AI.conclusion: Some AGN hosts may follow alternative evolutionary pathways in which star formation suppression precedes substantial structural compaction, in addition to the standard compaction-quenching channel.

title: Gaia DR3 Reveals the Kinematics of Young Stellar Objects in the Carina Nebula: Peripheral Expansion and Central Rotation
comment: 14 pages, 6 figures, Accepted by AJ
summary: We investigate the kinematics of the Carina Nebula using a sample of young stellar objects (YSOs) cross-matched with Gaia DR3, together with $^{12}\mathrm{CO}\,(1\mbox{--}0)$ molecular gas observations and APOGEE radial-velocity data. The results show that the proper motions of the YSOs in the four peripheral subregions of Carina display a systematic outward expansion, and that the two-dimensional expansion velocities of the subregions are approximately $0.57\mbox{--}4.56~\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$. The YSOs in the Central Region exhibit ordered rotation around an axis at a position angle of $86.9\pm1.5^\circ$, with a rotation velocity of $1.75\pm0.03~\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$. Further momentum estimates suggest that the current expansion in the peripheral regions may result from the combined effects of feedback from massive OB stars and possible past supernova explosions. These results indicate that feedback from massive stars plays a dominant role in the dynamical evolution of the giant molecular cloud in the Carina Nebula.

AI.tldr: The Carina Nebula's YSO subregions show systematic outward expansion while its Central Region rotates about an axis at P.A. 86.9°, indicating massive-star feedback dominates the GMC's dynamical evolution.
AI.motivation: The dynamical state and driving mechanisms of the giant molecular cloud in the Carina Nebula remain poorly constrained; the authors aim to characterize its kinematics (expansion vs. rotation) and identify the dominant feedback processes.
AI.method: Cross-match young stellar objects with Gaia DR3 proper motions, combining with 12CO(1-0) molecular gas observations and APOGEE radial velocities to map the 2D velocity field and estimate momentum.
AI.result: Four peripheral subregions show systematic outward expansion at 0.57-4.56 km/s; the Central Region shows ordered rotation about an axis at P.A. 86.9+/-1.5 deg with 1.75+/-0.03 km/s. Momentum estimates suggest peripheral expansion arises from OB-star feedback plus possible past supernovae.
AI.conclusion: Massive-star feedback plays a dominant role in the dynamical evolution of the Carina Nebula giant molecular cloud.

title: Primary and Secondary Star Formation in the Spiral Waves of NGC 628
comment: 32 pages, 14 figures, accepted by ApJ
summary: To determine the role of spiral arms and stellar feedback on the formation of stars, we examine the positions of optically identified and emerging star clusters in NGC 628. We find that the youngest clusters extend further into the spiral arms at small radii than at large radii, as expected when the angular flow rate through a wave-like arm increases with greater distance from corotation. The embedded or emerging star clusters (eYSCs) are identified relative to four distinct morphological features in the 7.7 micron image: spiral arm filaments, spiral arm spurs, spiral interarm feathers, and bubbles. Spiral arm-related eYSCs are presumably first-generation stars made from interstellar gas that was directly compressed by the density wave, while clusters along the rims of bubbles are secondary generations produced by feedback compression. The mass functions of the first and second generations differ: eYSCs in spiral arm filaments extend to significantly higher masses than eYSCs in bubbles. Secondary star formation continues downstream from primary star formation, removing the expected age gradient through the arms. Bubble eYSCs account for approximately one-third of all the emerging cluster mass. The outer arms have a more mixed distribution of spiral- and bubble-related eYSCs than the inner arms, potentially providing a way to distinguish wave and material arms and to find corotation in wave-like arms. Among the 17 most massive clusters with log M(Msun)>4, eight of them are in four tight pairs; in at least one case, the dynamical time for the pair is comparable to the cluster ages.

AI.tldr: Optically identified and emerging star clusters in NGC 628 reveal that first-generation clusters form along spiral arm filaments via density-wave compression, while secondary clusters form in bubble rims via feedback, with differing mass functions and mixed distributions in outer arms.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to determine the roles of spiral arms and stellar feedback in star formation by examining where optically identified and emerging star clusters form relative to spiral structures in NGC 628.
AI.method: They compare cluster positions across radius, finding youngest clusters extend further into arms at small radii (consistent with angular flow rate through a wave-like arm increasing with distance from corotation). Emerging clusters (eYSCs) are classified relative to four morphological features in the 7.7 micron image: spiral arm filaments, spurs, interarm feathers, and bubbles.
AI.result: Spiral-arm eYSCs are first-generation stars from gas compressed by the density wave, while bubble-rim clusters are secondary generations from feedback compression. Mass functions differ: arm-filament eYSCs reach significantly higher masses than bubble eYSCs. Secondary star formation downstream erases the expected age gradient through arms. Bubble eYSCs contribute ~one-third of emerging cluster mass. Outer arms show a more mixed distribution, potentially distinguishing wave from material arms and locating corotation. Among the 17 most massive clusters (log M>4), eight form four tight pairs, with at least one pair's dynamical time comparable to cluster ages.
AI.conclusion: Spiral arms (density-wave compression) and stellar feedback jointly drive star formation, producing distinct first- and second-generation cluster populations with different mass functions; the mixed outer-arm distribution may help identify corotation and arm type.

title: The dwarf galaxy NGC 185: the flagship of Andromeda's dwarf galaxies for the study of evolved multiple stellar populations
comment: 12 pages, 12 figures, accepted for publication on Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary:
Reaching galaxies at 10-15 Mpc with HST and JWST requires star
  formation history (SFH) diagnostics that do not rely on the faint
  main sequence turn-off. We investigate whether horizontal branch (HB),
  red clump (RC), and red and asymptotic giant branch (RGB, AGB) stars can
  fill this role for dwarf elliptical galaxies, using NGC 185 as a test case.
  We use stellar evolution models of low- and intermediate-mass stars as inputs
  to population synthesis simulations that reproduce the colour distribution and
  luminosity function of stars in the (mF606W-mF814W, mF814W)
  diagram. The study of the stars populating the HB is used to derive
  the distance modulus and reddening, the average mass loss suffered by the stars during
  the ascending on the RGB and the SFH occurred during the ancient epochs, before 7 Gyr ago.
  The luminosity function of the RC gives us constraints on the recent SFH (<8 Gyr).
  The distribution of HB stars yields a reddening E(B-V)=0.20 mag and a distance
  modulus DM=24.10 mag for NGC 185. The average mass lost by low-mass stars during
  the RGB phase is 0.22 +- 0.01 Msun. Star formation
  was concentrated at early epochs, with half of the stars formed more than 11 Gyr ago.
  The morphology of the HB indicates essentially no metallicity spread among stars older
  than 8 Gyr, whereas the slope of the RGB suggests that part of the stars younger than
  5-6 Gyr are slightly enriched in metals. Once RGB mass loss is adequately constrained, evolved stars can provide a
  reliable SFH for dwarf elliptical galaxies well beyond the reach of MSTO-based methods.
  We discuss the implications for more distant systems and the remaining uncertainties in
  the underlying stellar models.

AI.tldr: Evolved stars (HB, RC, RGB, AGB) instead of the faint MSTO can recover the star formation history, distance, reddening, and RGB mass loss of dwarf ellipticals; applied to NGC 185, giving E(B-V)=0.20, DM=24.10, RGB mass loss 0.22 Msun, and an ancient-dominated SFH.
AI.motivation: Reaching galaxies at 10–15 Mpc with HST/JWST makes the main sequence turn-off too faint to use for star formation history diagnostics, so alternative, brighter stellar tracers are needed.
AI.method: Uses stellar evolution models of low- and intermediate-mass stars as inputs to population synthesis simulations that reproduce the colour distribution and luminosity function in the (mF606W−mF814W, mF814W) CMD of the dwarf elliptical NGC 185, exploiting HB, RC, RGB, and AGB stars.
AI.result: HB morphology gives E(B-V)=0.20 mag and DM=24.10 mag; average RGB mass loss of low-mass stars is 0.22±0.01 Msun; star formation was concentrated at early epochs with half the stars older than 11 Gyr; HB morphology shows essentially no metallicity spread above 8 Gyr, while the RGB slope indicates slight metal enrichment among stars younger than 5–6 Gyr.
AI.conclusion: Once RGB mass loss is adequately constrained, evolved stars can provide a reliable SFH for dwarf ellipticals well beyond MSTO-based reach; implications for more distant systems and remaining uncertainties in the stellar models are discussed.

title: Living near filaments: How environment shapes age profiles in low-mass galaxies
comment: 6 pages including appendices. Submitted to A&A
summary: U-shaped radial age profiles have recently been reported in low-mass galaxies. This type of profile differs from the usually observed positive radial age gradients of the low-mass regime. We aim to characterise the environment in which low-mass galaxies with U-shaped age profiles are more commonly found. We use the IllustrisTNG-50 hydrodynamical simulations to select a sample of galaxies with stellar masses ranging from $10^9 \, M_\odot$ to $10^{10} \, M_\odot$. Based on their radial age profiles, we classify the sample into galaxies with and without a U-shaped feature. We define a U-shaped profile as one where stellar ages decrease towards a local minimum and subsequently increase, requiring an age contrast of at least 0.4 Gyr on either side of the minimum relative to its value. We find 145 galaxies with U-shaped age profiles ($\sim 11\%$ of the sample). They are mostly central systems ($\sim 72\%$) and $\sim 82\%$ of them reside within low-mass halos ($M_{200} < 10^{12} \, M_\odot$). We also find that galaxies exhibiting this feature are located at large distances from galaxy groups but close to cosmic filaments, with a median distance of $\sim 265$ kpc, whereas those without U-shaped age profiles tend to be located farther away from these structures ($\sim 351$ kpc).

AI.tldr: Using IllustrisTNG-50 simulations, ~11% of low-mass galaxies (10^9–10^10 M☉) show U-shaped radial age profiles; these are mostly central galaxies in low-mass halos located far from groups but close to cosmic filaments (~265 kpc vs ~351 kpc for those without the feature).
AI.motivation: U-shaped radial age profiles have recently been reported in low-mass galaxies, contrasting with the typically observed positive radial age gradients in this mass regime. The environmental conditions favoring such profiles are unclear, motivating a characterization of the environment in which low-mass galaxies with U-shaped age profiles are more commonly found.
AI.method: Select galaxies with stellar masses 10^9–10^10 M☉ from the IllustrisTNG-50 hydrodynamical simulations and classify them by radial age profile into those with and without a U-shaped feature. A U-shaped profile is defined as stellar ages decreasing to a local minimum then increasing, requiring a minimum age contrast of 0.4 Gyr on either side of the minimum. Environmental properties (central/satellite status, host halo mass, distance to galaxy groups and cosmic filaments) are then compared between the two classes.
AI.result: 145 galaxies (~11% of the sample) exhibit U-shaped age profiles. They are predominantly central systems (~72%), and ~82% reside in low-mass halos (M_200 < 10^12 M☉). Galaxies with the feature lie at large distances from galaxy groups but close to cosmic filaments (median ~265 kpc), whereas those without it are farther from these structures (median ~351 kpc).
AI.conclusion: U-shaped radial age profiles in low-mass galaxies are preferentially associated with central galaxies in low-mass halos situated at large group-centric distances yet near cosmic filaments, suggesting that filament-adjacent, group-peripheral environments favor this age-profile morphology.

title: Investigating the initial conditions of globular clusters via $N$-body simulations: I. half-mass radius and stellar density
summary: Born out of the turbulent, dense gas of the early Universe, globular clusters (GCs) represent a significantly different star-formation mode compared to the local Universe. To quantify the initial cluster conditions, we perform the long-term dynamical evolution of GCs using the high-precision direct N-body simulation code PeTar. As the first step in a series of studies, we investigate the two low-mass outer-halo GCs, Eridanus and Whiting 1. By comparing simulated number density profiles with observations, we derive best-fit initial half-mass radii of $2.0 \pm 1.0$ pc for Eridanus and $2.5 \pm 0.5$ pc for Whiting 1, corresponding to initial surface densities of $2592.03 M_\odot pc^{-2}$ and $226.35 M_\odot pc^{-2}$, respectively -- 2-3 orders of magnitude higher than their present-day values. The absence of multiple populations (MPs) in Whiting 1 and young massive clusters (YMCs), in contrast to the MP-hosting Eridanus, supports the scenario that MP formation requires higher initial surface density and/or lower metallicity. Using the simulations as a template, we identify five high-probability extra-tidal candidates of Whiting 1 from Gaia DR3 and APOGEE DR17, which exhibit coherent kinematics and chemical abundances. Our results demonstrate that the diffuse states of low-mass GCs are the product of long-term dynamical expansion and tidal stripping, and that their primordial configurations were significantly denser.

AI.tldr: Long-term direct N-body simulations of two low-mass outer-halo globular clusters infer dense primordial configurations, showing their present diffuse states arise from dynamical expansion and tidal stripping and linking multiple-population formation to high initial surface density.
AI.motivation: Globular clusters formed under early-Universe conditions distinct from local star formation, and their initial properties are poorly constrained. The authors aim to quantify the initial cluster conditions of low-mass outer-halo GCs and connect them to multiple-population formation and present-day diffuse structure.
AI.method: High-precision direct N-body simulations with the PeTar code evolved long-term for Eridanus and Whiting 1. Best-fit initial half-mass radii were obtained by matching simulated number density profiles to observations. Simulations also served as templates to search for extra-tidal members in Gaia DR3 and APOGEE DR17 data.
AI.result: Best-fit initial half-mass radii are 2.0 ± 1.0 pc (Eridanus) and 2.5 ± 0.5 pc (Whiting 1), with initial surface densities of 2592.03 and 226.35 M_sun pc^-2, i.e. 2-3 orders of magnitude above present values. The lack of multiple populations in Whiting 1 and young massive clusters versus MP-hosting Eridanus supports MP formation requiring higher initial surface density and/or lower metallicity. Five high-probability extra-tidal candidates for Whiting 1 with coherent kinematics and abundances were identified.
AI.conclusion: Low-mass GCs' diffuse states result from long-term dynamical expansion and tidal stripping, and their primordial configurations were substantially denser than today. Initial surface density (and metallicity) appears to govern multiple-population formation.

title: Euclid Quick Data Release (Q1). Refining the strong lens sample with Space Warps crowd-sourced science
comment: 16 pages, 9 figures, submitted to A&A
summary: We demonstrate the efficacy of crowd-sourced refinement of strong gravitational lens candidate samples by citizen scientists. Binary (lens/non-lens) classification by citizen scientists has been conducted previously, and here we extend such categorisation into `definite', `probable', `possible', and `non-lenses'. This grading is a required stage ahead of any strong lens sample publication and is usually carried out by (small) teams of researchers. We compare the responses of the volunteers to those of strong lens researchers and discuss the optimal strategy for lens classification and grading in future strong lens searches. Volunteers are found to be able to correctly identify systems of each grade, and their responses can be calibrated to be comparable to those of researchers. Grade posteriors, defined as the probability that a strong lens system classified by the volunteers is a certain grade, converge most rapidly for non-lens systems. We find that one researcher classification is equivalent to only 1.9 volunteer classifications when grading such systems. There is significant disagreement in the grading of intermediate-grade lens candidates amongst both volunteers and researchers. Moving towards calibrated lens probabilities for future lens searches would help to account for such subjectivity. If the Q1 lens search was rerun with volunteers performing lens grading (and corresponding calibration), a completeness of 79% for Grades A+B (corresponding to definite + probable lenses respectively) could be achieved with 41% purity prior to researcher inspection - this would correspond to an expected 12500 true lenses (i.e. excluding contaminants) in Euclid DR1.

AI.tldr: Citizen scientists can reliably grade strong gravitational lens candidates into definite/probable/possible/non-lens classes, with responses calibratable to researcher level; one researcher classification is equivalent to about 1.9 volunteer classifications.
AI.motivation: Strong lens sample publication requires candidate grading, which is traditionally done by small researcher teams—a costly bottleneck for large surveys. Prior citizen-science work only performed binary lens/non-lens classification, so it is unclear whether volunteers can handle the finer multi-grade categorisation needed and how their responses compare to experts.
AI.method: Extend crowd-sourced lens search from binary classification to four grades (definite, probable, possible, non-lens). Compare volunteer responses to those of strong lens researchers, examine grade posteriors (probability a volunteer-classified system is of a given grade), quantify the volunteer-to-researcher equivalence ratio, and assess grading disagreement across intermediate grades. Also project performance if the Q1 lens search were rerun with volunteers performing calibrated grading.
AI.result: Volunteers correctly identify systems of each grade, and their responses can be calibrated to match researcher assessments. Grade posteriors converge most rapidly for non-lens systems. One researcher classification equals only 1.9 volunteer classifications when grading. Significant disagreement exists among both volunteers and researchers for intermediate-grade candidates. Rerunning Q1 with volunteer grading yields 79% completeness for Grades A+B at 41% purity before researcher inspection, corresponding to an expected 12,500 true lenses in Euclid DR1.
AI.conclusion: Crowd-sourced grading is an effective, scalable substitute for small-team researcher grading in strong lens searches. Moving toward calibrated lens probabilities would mitigate subjectivity in intermediate grades, and volunteer pre-grading can substantially increase lens yield in future surveys such as Euclid.

title: Magnetic Properties of Galactic Molecular Clouds
comment: 38 pages, 10 figures, accepted by The Astrophysical Journal
summary: The earliest studies of molecular clouds (MCs) showed scaling relations between mass and radius M$\sim$R^s with exponent s $\approx$ 2, known as the third Larson relation. More recent CO surveys indicate 2 < s < 3 in the inner Milky Way (MW) and nearby galaxies. These observations appear consistent with the virial equilibrium (VE) of magnetically subcritical clouds, bound by the pressure Pe of the midplane ISM. The VE equations for such clouds are consistent with 2 < s < 3 for magnetically subcritical clouds, but not for magnetically critical, supercritical, or nonmagnetic clouds. We fit the subcritical VE equations to M-R trends observed in CO surveys of $\sim$1500 clouds, with correlation coefficients 0.8 - 1. The fits indicate median mass-to-flux ratio lambda $\approx$ 0.7, magnetic field strength Btot $\approx$ 60$\mathrm{μG}$, and Pe/k $\approx$ 5 x 10^5 cm^-3 K in the inner MW, with lesser values in M33 and M31. For 18 MW "bones," VE analysis assuming likely values of Pe also indicates subcritical values of lambda, as found from polarization observations. These results indicate that many giant molecular clouds (GMCs) are consistent with pressure-bound magnetically subcritical virial equilibrium. If so, GMCs may have low star formation efficiency (SFE) because their relatively strong fields cause filaments, clumps and cores to form slowly, while feedback and turbulence disperse them rapidly. The fields in their clumps and cores are likely weak enough to allow star-forming collapse, according to Zeeman and DCF observations, and according to MHD simulations which predict SFE $\approx$ 0.5-2%.

AI.tldr: Mass–radius scaling of molecular clouds (M∼R^s, 2<s<3) is consistent with virial equilibrium of pressure-bound, magnetically subcritical clouds; fits to ~1500 CO clouds give λ≈0.7, B≈60 μG, and P_e/k≈5×10^5 cm^-3 K, implying low star formation efficiency in GMCs.
AI.motivation: The classical third Larson relation (s≈2) is contradicted by recent CO surveys showing 2<s<3, and the physical origin of this steeper scaling — and its implication for cloud evolution and star formation — remains unsettled.
AI.method: Derive virial equilibrium equations for magnetically subcritical clouds confined by external midplane ISM pressure, show these yield 2<s<3 (unlike critical, supercritical, or nonmagnetic cases), and fit them to M–R trends from CO surveys of ~1500 clouds; cross-check with virial analysis of 18 Milky Way "bones" and comparison to polarization, Zeeman, and DCF measurements plus MHD simulations.
AI.result: Fits achieve correlation coefficients of 0.8–1 and give median mass-to-flux ratio λ≈0.7, total field strength B_tot≈60 μG, and P_e/k≈5×10^5 cm^-3 K in the inner Milky Way, with lower values in M33 and M31; the 18 bones also indicate subcritical λ, consistent with polarization observations. MHD simulations predict SFE≈0.5–2%.
AI.conclusion: Many giant molecular clouds are consistent with pressure-bound, magnetically subcritical virial equilibrium; their relatively strong fields slow filament/clump/core formation while feedback and turbulence disperse them, explaining low SFE, whereas fields in clumps and cores remain weak enough to permit collapse.

title: ReveaLLAGN 3: Revealing the Infrared Spectral Energy Distributions of Low Luminosity AGN
summary: The spectral energy distributions of active galactic nuclei (AGN) provide valuable information on the emission mechanisms taking place in their inner regions. Here we use the James Webb Space Telescope to study the near and mid-infrared spectral energy distributions of seven nearby low-luminosity active galaxy nuclei from 1.7 to 24 $μm$. We cleanly separate the AGN spectrum by performing spatial fits of the two-dimensional images across all wavelengths. We then compare these clean unresolved spectra to aperture-based spectra and show that they effectively remove galaxy contamination. Comparing our infrared measurements to X-ray emission, we find that low-luminosity AGN have enhanced near-infrared emission relative to more luminous AGN, a trend that correlates with radio-loudness, while their mid-infrared-to-X-ray ratios are comparable. A majority of our targets show strong compact silicate emission suggesting the presence of warm dust on parsec scales in these systems. We also quantify the near- and mid-infrared power-law slopes and colors of low-luminosity AGN. In the near-infrared we find AGN of all luminosities have similar spectral slopes and colors, however in the mid-infrared, we find low-luminosity AGN typically have steeper slopes and redder colors than more luminous AGN. Both the strong silicate emission and steep mid-infrared slopes disagree with existing models for low-luminosity AGN spectral energy distributions.

AI.tldr: JWST spatially resolves the near- to mid-IR SEDs of seven nearby low-luminosity AGN (1.7–24 μm), revealing enhanced near-IR emission, strong compact silicate emission, and steeper mid-IR slopes than luminous AGN—findings that challenge current low-luminosity AGN SED models.
AI.motivation: AGN spectral energy distributions (SEDs) encode the emission mechanisms in their inner regions, but low-luminosity AGN are poorly characterized, and existing SED models may not capture their IR properties. The authors aim to obtain clean, uncontaminated IR spectra of low-luminosity AGN to test these models.
AI.method: JWST near- and mid-IR observations (1.7–24 μm) of seven nearby low-luminosity AGN. The AGN spectrum is isolated via spatial fits of 2D images at all wavelengths, producing clean unresolved spectra that are compared with aperture-based spectra. The IR measurements are then compared with X-ray emission, and near-/mid-IR power-law slopes and colors are quantified.
AI.result: The clean unresolved spectra effectively remove galaxy contamination. Relative to more luminous AGN, low-luminosity AGN show enhanced near-IR emission that correlates with radio loudness, while their mid-IR-to-X-ray ratios are comparable. Most targets exhibit strong compact silicate emission, indicating warm dust on parsec scales. Near-IR slopes and colors are similar across all luminosities; mid-IR slopes are steeper and colors redder for low-luminosity AGN.
AI.conclusion: Low-luminosity AGN differ systematically from luminous AGN in their IR SEDs, and both the strong silicate emission and steep mid-IR slopes are inconsistent with existing low-luminosity AGN SED models, motivating revised dust/emission prescriptions.
